narrative:
Your application was denied because the model predicts you have an 84% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, this means the university judged that you would very likely not pass the exam required to practice law, making admission a risky investment in your future.

The most important factor driving this decision was your class rank in your third year. You ranked in the first decile, meaning you were in the bottom 10% of your class. Students who are typically accepted sit much higher, around the sixth decile on average. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failing the bar exam.

Your first-year class rank was the second most influential factor. At the second decile, you were again well below the average sixth decile of accepted students. This pattern matters because it shows early academic struggles persisted through your third year, rather than improving over time.

The third strongest influence was your LSAT score of 30, notably lower than the average of about 37 for accepted students. A lower score suggests weaker foundational reasoning and reading skills, which are critical for bar exam success.

All three of these factors pushed the prediction in the same direction: toward failure. None of them pointed toward passing. Your family income, undergraduate GPA, gender, or race were not significant factors, and protected attributes like gender and race were not used in the prediction at all.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through dedicated preparation, as it is the most direct way to demonstrate readiness. You should also seek academic support or bar-exam preparation early in your legal studies to strengthen your performance in the first and third years, which are exactly the signals the model weighs most heavily.
